title: Back to it
hookLine: don't be disgusted when you fail; return, and be glad if most of what you do is decent (Meditations 5.9)
tomorrow: How am I using my soul?

lines: PICK IT UP, OR PULL IT ALL OUT?
cards: A knitter drops a stitch three rows back. There are two ways this can go. In one, there's a sigh, a crochet hook, the stitch is picked up, and the scarf carries on.
In the other, the whole thing is yanked off the needles in disgust and shoved in a drawer for a year. The dropped stitch is the same in both. The difference is the next minute.
In book five, entry nine, Marcus Aurelius writes to himself about exactly that minute.

teach.b: Don't be disgusted, discouraged or dissatisfied, Marcus tells himself, if you don't manage to do everything by right principles. He expects to fall short.
A man who wrote this much about virtue knew how often he missed it.
When you've been knocked off, he says, come back again. The whole practice is in that one word: not never fall, but return.

teach.h: CONTENT IF MOST OF IT IS DECENT.
teach.b: And be content if the greater part of what you do is worthy of a human being. Not all of it. The greater part.
Love the thing you're returning to. Then a lovely detail.
Don't go back to philosophy as if to a schoolmaster with a cane, he says, but the way people with sore eyes go back to a sponge and egg, or someone goes back to a soothing bandage or a warm compress.
Philosophy, for Marcus, is the medicine, not the punishment. You return because it helps. Now look at this week.
Good fortune: luck is in the bearing. The gulf of time: a life against eternity. Push it away: set the troubling thought down.
Fit for me: test the act, not the critics. What is mine: sincerity, dignity, endurance. The prescription: hard things as medicine.
And now, back to it. You'll forget most of these lines by Thursday. That's fine.
The practice was never to remember perfectly. It's to come back.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 5.9 after a lapse: no self-disgust, just a return to the practice, and contentment if most of their acts are decent.

o: the emperor who said: after a slip, return without disgust
a Roman teacher who corrected his students with a cane
a Roman general who said one failure ruins a whole campaign

games.q: back to it — tap the pairs.
p: not how to return to philosophy

s: Marcus expects to do everything by right principles
he tells himself not to be disgusted when he doesn't.
Marcus compares philosophy to a soothing remedy for sore eyes
a sponge and egg, a bandage, a warm compress, not a schoolmaster.
Marcus says be content only if all you do is good
he says be content if the greater part is worthy of a human.

games.q: you've meditated every day for two weeks, then miss three days. tonight you think: I've blown it. what fits Meditations 5.9?
o: start over next month, with a fresh streak.
sit tonight, a little, and be glad you returned.
games.why: Marcus: when you've been knocked off, come back; don't return as to a stern schoolmaster, but as to a soothing remedy.

practice: Think of one recent slip, and let the voice that comes with it, the disgust or the why bother, speak and pass. Then picture the next small step back into the habit, as if reaching for something soothing rather than something stern.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who told himself not to be disgusted when he fell short, but to return, and be content if the greater part was worthy. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'love of wisdom': what Marcus says to return to, as to a remedy, not a schoolmaster.

carryVoice: Your line: a sponge and egg. Philosophy is the compress, not the cane. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and another week.
